name: Anti-racism
summary: Anti-racism opposes racism and racial discrimination in law, institutions and ideas. Its programmatic texts (the UN's ICERD and Durban Declaration) reject doctrines of racial superiority as false, require states to prohibit discrimination including by private persons, allow time-limited special measures, and condemn colonialism and slavery; Kendi's structural account judges policies by whether they produce racial equity. It has no economic, constitutional or foreign-policy programme of its own beyond these.
scope: Mainstream anti-racism as stated in three bodies of text: the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (1965), the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (2001) adopted at the UN World Conference against Racism and Ibram X. Kendi's structural account (the How to Be an Antiracist excerpt and his 2019 NPR interviews, with Madva's scholarly summary of it). Madva (a philosophy paper on antiracists) is the scholarly source that names the ideology and Kendi; ICERD and the Durban texts use 'anti-racism' and 'racism' for the same cause. Excluded: Black Power and Black nationalism, socialist or feminist offshoots (the Combahee River Collective), and ethnic-nationalist movements. Their texts were not used, and the earlier audit's answers that rested on Wikipedia summaries or on those strands were nulled in this pass. Anti-racism has no stated programme on most economic, constitutional and foreign-policy questions, so those statements are null.

missingStatements.text: Governments should review and repeal laws and policies that perpetuate racial discrimination in effect, even where no discriminatory intent exists.
missingStatements.rationale: ICERD defines discrimination by its purpose or effect and Art. 2(1)(c) requires states to amend or nullify laws that create or perpetuate it.

missingStatements.text: A policy should be judged racist if it produces racial inequity, whatever its intent.
missingStatements.rationale: Kendi defines racist policy as any policy that creates inequitable outcomes between racial groups, and the structural view treats intent as secondary.

notes: Themes searched in ICERD, the Durban Declaration and Kendi's texts: race and racism, special measures, colonialism and slavery, reparations and apologies, migration, indigenous peoples, hate speech and the internet, education, policing and justice, development and debt, democracy and political participation, language, gender, religion, Israel/Palestine. The Durban texts speak of reparation for victims of discrimination but only 'note' that some states paid reparation for slavery and colonialism, so the reparations statements are null. Statements on markets, ownership, taxes, guns, the family, religion in public life, war and most constitutional design have no position in these texts and are null; the earlier pass's 0 answers there recorded adherents differing, which is silence. King's Letter from Birmingham Jail was read, but no defining source ties it to anti-racism (the source check fails), so the answers resting on it were nulled; the Combahee statement and Carmichael's Black Power address were set aside as other movements' sources. Kendi's 2019 Politico proposal for an anti-racist constitutional amendment and a Department of Anti-racism was read; it settles no statement (a proposal limited to racial inequity, not a general position on experts or courts). Kendi's book itself was not available as full text; his positions come from the Penguin excerpt, two NPR interviews and Madva's scholarly report. This pass nulled answers resting on Wikipedia summaries (reviewHistory keeps the earlier versions) and is expected to leave the ideology below the uncertainty rule: that is the honest result of the record.
